notes: Five structures selected from Tobias's taxonomy for maximal structural distance from one another while remaining applicable across genre and budget. Each defines a different relationship between protagonist, conflict, information and time — which is what makes two variants genuinely different, rather than the same story with different names. Assignment happens before generation; the generator fills a container it did not choose.

items.label: The Crucible
items.premise: A small group is confined together and cannot leave until the conflict between them resolves. Pressure, not plot, produces the revelations.

structural_blueprint.description: An event places the characters in a space they cannot leave without cost, and establishes what each one wants from the others.
The group organises itself around a shared task or pretence that temporarily holds.
Pressure forces disclosure. Each revelation makes the previous arrangement untenable.
One character must choose between self-protection and the group, with no option that costs nothing.
The situation resolves through what was admitted, not through escape or rescue.

citations: Tobias, R.B. (1993), 20 Master Plots and How to Build Them, Writer's Digest Books

items.label: Ensemble Convergence
items.premise: Several characters pursue independent goals that turn out to intersect at a single event. The structure's meaning lives in the intersection, not in any one thread.

structural_blueprint.description: Each thread establishes its protagonist, their goal and the pressure on them, in isolation from the others.
Two threads touch in a way that neither party recognises as significant.
Each thread's progress makes another thread's problem worse.
All threads arrive at the same place and time, and the collision is unavoidable.
The outcome is settled by the combination of choices, not by any single character's decision.

citations: Tobias, R.B. (1993), 20 Master Plots and How to Build Them, Writer's Digest Books

items.label: Non-Linear Revelation
items.premise: A concealed truth is disclosed out of chronological order, so that the audience's understanding is repeatedly re-framed. Location count is set by the telling present, not by the revealed past.

structural_blueprint.description: The present establishes an unexplained situation and someone with a reason to explain it.
A fragment of the past is disclosed that appears to explain the present, and does so incorrectly.
Further fragments complicate rather than confirm, and the reliability of the source comes into question.
A disclosure changes the meaning of everything already shown without contradicting it.
The full truth arrives and the present-day character must act on it.

citations: Tobias, R.B. (1993), 20 Master Plots and How to Build Them, Writer's Digest Books
Propp, V. (1928), Morphology of the Folktale — narrative function theory

items.label: Pursuit
items.premise: One party chases another, and each act narrows the distance and raises the cost of being caught. At the lowest budget the pursuit is psychological rather than physical.

structural_blueprint.description: The pursuit begins and the terms are established: who wants what, and what happens if they get it.
The pursued escapes at a cost that reduces their options.
Each subsequent evasion is harder and costs more, while the pursuer learns.
The pursuit appears to end in the pursuer's favour, and the pursued's last resource is exposed.
The chase stops and is settled directly, on terms set by what the pursuit revealed.

citations: Tobias, R.B. (1993), 20 Master Plots and How to Build Them, Writer's Digest Books

items.label: Transformation Arc
items.premise: A single protagonist changes in a specific, nameable way, driven by external events that make their existing behaviour stop working.

structural_blueprint.description: The protagonist's habitual behaviour is shown working well enough to explain why they keep it.
An event removes the conditions under which that behaviour succeeded.
The protagonist applies the old approach harder, and it fails more expensively.
A loss the protagonist cannot rationalise forces recognition.
The protagonist acts differently under comparable pressure, demonstrating the change rather than stating it.
The changed behaviour settles into a new normal, with what it cost made visible.

citations: Tobias, R.B. (1993), 20 Master Plots and How to Build Them, Writer's Digest Books
Xu, W. et al. (2025), Echoes in AI: Quantifying Lack of Plot Diversity in LLM Outputs, arXiv 2501.00273
